title: It rains on the Sun: glowing plasma pours down arcs up to five Earths tall

cover.alt: Bright orange loops of glowing plasma arch out from the edge of the Sun against a dark red background.
cover.credit: NASA Goddard SVS/SDO Science Team/Virtual Solar Observatory · Public domain

body: On 19 July 2012, after a solar flare and an eruption on the edge of the Sun, million-degree plasma in its outer atmosphere began to cool and condense. Because the plasma is electrically charged, it can’t simply drop: it is forced to move along the Sun’s invisible magnetic field lines. So it streamed back to the surface along giant arcs, some as tall as **five Earths** stacked up. This downpour, called coronal rain, lasted for hours, and it lets scientists see the shape of magnetic fields that are otherwise invisible.

slides.alt: Time-lapse in orange ultraviolet light: a tangle of bright loops arches off the edge of the Sun, with glowing strands of plasma sliding down along them.
slides.caption: 19 July 2012, 07:30 to 09:30 UTC, six minutes per second: NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory watches plasma rain down along magnetic loops after a flare.
slides.credit: NASA Goddard SVS/SDO Science Team/Virtual Solar Observatory · Public domain · excerpt

slides.heading: How it rains on the Sun

steps.label: A flare and an eruption shake the region
It condenses along magnetic field lines
It slides down the lines to the surface

slides.label: stacked up: the height of the tallest arcs of rain
slides.text: The display lasted hours. It was set off by two eruptions: a solar flare and a coronal mass ejection, which hurled material out into space.

slides.prompt: The Solar Dynamics Observatory saw the rain in ultraviolet light of wavelength 304 ångströms. What temperature does that light pick out?
slides.detail: Cool, by the standards of the corona: the plasma started out at around a million degrees before it condensed.

slides.question: Why does coronal rain fall along arcs instead of straight down?
options: The Sun’s spin flings it sideways
slides.explanation: The plasma is electrically charged, so it is forced to move along the Sun’s magnetic field lines, tracing their loops as it falls.
